Spinycheek lanternfish Benthosema fibulatum is a mesopelagic myctophid widely distributed in tropical and subtropical waters, where it undergoes pronounced diel vertical migrations. Recent field studies examining growth trajectories have documented that individuals reach a maximum standard length of 10 centimeters [Li = 10 centimeters], a size that appears to represent an asymptotic upper bound for this species within its range. This ultimate length is attained gradually over the course of several years, with growth rates modulated by local thermal conditions and prey availability. Specimens collected during midwater trawling surveys in the Pacific consistently approach this upper limit, while larger individuals are rarely encountered, suggesting that size-selective predation or senescent mortality truncates the size distribution near this value. The pronounced photophore pattern characteristic of sexually mature adults becomes fully developed well before this terminal size is achieved, with the onset of reproductive capability occurring at a considerably smaller body dimension. Comparative data from related myctophid genera indicate that a 10 centimeter maximum length is relatively modest for the family, though it aligns closely with the typical size range observed in other members of the genus Benthosema. This length also serves as the basis for allometric equations used to estimate body mass and other life-history correlates.

The onset of sexual maturation in Benthosema fibulatum has been examined through histological analysis of gonadal tissue from trawl-caught specimens, revealing that individuals first become reproductively competent at a standard length of 4 centimeters [Lp = 4 centimeters]. This size threshold marks the transition from a strictly somatic growth phase to one in which energy is also directed toward gamete production. At this length, the wet body mass averages approximately 0.65 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.65 grams], reflecting the relatively slender, streamlined body plan typical of vertically migrating myctophids. The mass-at-length relationship used to derive this value follows a power-law function calibrated from preserved and fresh specimens, yielding consistent estimates across multiple sampling seasons. Puberty at such a modest size, roughly 40 percent of the ultimate length, suggests an early onset of reproductive activity relative to the overall growth trajectory. This pattern is consistent with an opportunistic life-history strategy common among small pelagic fishes inhabiting variable environments, where early maturity enhances the probability of contributing offspring before encountering episodes of high mortality. The transition to reproductive status also coincides with changes in diel vertical migration behavior, as maturing individuals begin to allocate more time to foraging in productive surface waters.

Under the thermal conditions characteristic of its natural habitat, approximately 8.9 °C [T = approximately 8.9 °C], gravid females of Benthosema fibulatum produce about 10.6 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = about 10.6 eggs per spawning event] with a spawning frequency of approximately one event per day [F_R_i = approximately one event per day]. This high daily output, equivalent to a maximum reproductive rate of roughly 3,869 eggs per year [Ri = roughly 3,869 eggs per year], reflects the upper limit of oocyte production and release under optimal feeding conditions. The elevated reproductive investment is consistent with the species' life-history strategy, channeling a substantial proportion of available resources into gamete production once maturity is attained. Such a strategy is advantageous in oligotrophic environments where the window of opportunity for larval survival may be brief and unpredictable. The thermal condition used in these trials mirrors the temperature range encountered by adults during their nighttime forays into epipelagic waters, where spawning is believed to occur. Field validation of these laboratory-derived rates remains an active area of investigation, as in situ observations of spawning events are inherently difficult to obtain for mesopelagic species.

At the commencement of exogenous feeding, newly hatched larvae of Benthosema fibulatum are extremely small, with a wet weight at birth of just 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams]. This minute mass corresponds to an egg diameter of approximately 1 millimeter, a typical value for the genus Benthosema, and reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the developing embryo. The larval body is nearly transparent at this stage, with a yolk sac that sustains the individual during the first few days before the mouth opens and the digestive tract becomes functional. The extremely low birth mass places Benthosema fibulatum among the smaller offspring producers within the Myctophidae, a family already characterized by relatively modest egg sizes compared to many other marine teleosts. This initial mass imposes a critical constraint on early survival, as larvae must encounter suitably sized prey within a narrow window following yolk-sac resorption. Mortality during this period is exceptionally high, a common feature among fishes with planktonic larval stages, and the small initial size likely contributes to the species' overall population dynamics. The relationship between egg size, larval size at hatching, and subsequent growth rates remains an important focus for understanding recruitment variability in this species.

Longevity in Benthosema fibulatum has been estimated from the analysis of otolith microincrements, which provide a reliable record of daily growth in mesopelagic fishes. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species is approximately 547.5 days [am = approximately 547.5 days], a value that corresponds to roughly one and a half years under the thermal conditions typical of its habitat, approximately 8.9 °C [T = approximately 8.9 °C]. This relatively short lifespan places Benthosema fibulatum among the faster-living myctophids, consistent with its early maturation and high reproductive output. The ultimate wet weight associated with this lifespan is approximately 11.22 grams [Wwi = approximately 11.22 grams], a value derived from the allometric length-mass relationship established for the species. Mortality rates increase markedly after the first year, with very few individuals persisting beyond 18 months in wild populations. Comparisons with congeneric species, such as Benthosema suborbitale, reveal a similar pattern of rapid growth and early senescence, suggesting that this tempo of life is evolutionarily conserved within the genus.
